Using that for a Costco trip would be wrong three times over. It fabricates
receipts that never existed. It destroys a match to express a reporting
preference. And because `detectDuplicates` keys on `amount|date` alone
(`duplicateDetection.ts:25`), an evenly-divided receipt immediately flags both
halves as Potential Duplicates on the very page you divided it.

So the first change is vocabulary:

| | divides a purchase across | touches the match? | frequency |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Partial Charge** (was _Split Receipt_) | **Transactions** | clears it, deliberately | rare |
| **Category Split** (new) | **Categories** | never | every Costco trip |

Both names say what is being divided, and "split" survives only in the qualified
form. See the glossary entries in [Domain model](../domain-model.md).

## Stage 0 — the rename

Pure rename, no behaviour change, done first so nothing new is written in the old
vocabulary.

- 411 occurrences of "split" outside the `.split()` string method, concentrated in
  three files: `ReceiptService.split.spec.ts` (145), `reconciliation/+page.svelte`
  (98), `ReceiptService.ts` (58).
- `receipts.split_group_id` → `charge_group_id` (baseline `:610`) and
  `idx_receipts_split_group_id` → `idx_receipts_charge_group_id` (`:781`). Both are
  metadata-only DDL — no data rewrite. There are **no generated Supabase types**;
  the models are hand-written (`src/lib/models/Receipt.ts`), so the DB surface is
  exactly those two objects plus 52 code references.
- The 11 `#{#spl*}` spec tags. Renaming scheme still open — see below.
- The hand-maintained baseline needs the two lines edited to match. Verify with
  `npm run db:reset`.

**This is a breaking change with no compatibility window.** Vercel deploys on push;
`supabase db push` is a separate manual step, so code and schema disagree in
between. The blast radius is narrow and was checked: every read is `select('*')`,
so reads degrade silently to a `null` field, and only _writes_ of the column fail —
Partial Charge creation and its "N of M" badge. Nothing else in the app touches it.
Accepted rather than staged as expand-and-contract; push the migration as soon as
the deploy is green.

## The model

**An Expense becomes a categorized _portion_ of a Receipt.** A Receipt yields one
Expense per Category Split, and exactly one — carrying the whole total — when
nobody has split it, so the common case still reads 1:1.

The Receipt is untouched. `total_amount` and `matched_transaction_id` are off
limits to this feature, which is why **reconciliation needs no changes at all**.

### One split is the remainder

You split by **carving off the exceptions**, not by describing every part. A Costco
trip already auto-categorized Groceries takes two actions to become
$150 Groceries / $60 Household / $30 Clothing, not three: you carve off Household
and Clothing, and Groceries keeps what is left.

The remainder is **the row the Receipt already had**. Two things follow, and they
are the reason this design is cheap:

- **No backfill.** Every row in `expense_categories` today is already a valid
  remainder with no siblings. The migration is additive and the existing data is
  correct by construction.
- **`categorization_source` survives.** A vendor rule's `auto` assignment is not
  silently converted to a manual one by carving $60 off it.

### The remainder is computed, never stored

`amount IS NULL` means "whatever is left" — `total_amount` minus its siblings,
resolved at read time.

The deciding case is editing the receipt total. OCR reads $240; you carve off $60
Household; someone later corrects the total to $260 — and totals are editable from
**three** surfaces (the edit modal, the Expenses page, the Receipts page). With a
stored remainder the parts still sum to $240 against a $260 receipt and **nothing
errors**; the report quietly loses $20. Defined as what is left, the remainder
becomes $200 by construction. The same argument kills rounding drift: $10 in three
parts always adds up.

The cost: `NULL` is a magic value needing a partial unique index, and **resolving
the remainder is a computation that must live in exactly one place**
(`ExpenseService`) or it will be reimplemented in the report, the exporters and the
split modal. `applyRuleToVisibleExpenses` exists today precisely because two pages
needed the same logic.

### Schema

```sql
ALTER TABLE expense_categories ADD COLUMN amount numeric;      -- NULL = the remainder
ALTER TABLE expense_categories DROP CONSTRAINT expense_categories_pkey;
ALTER TABLE expense_categories ADD COLUMN id uuid PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid();
ALTER TABLE expense_categories ADD CONSTRAINT expense_categories_receipt_category_unique
  UNIQUE (receipt_id, category_id);
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX expense_categories_one_remainder
  ON expense_categories (receipt_id) WHERE amount IS NULL;
```

`receipts.total_amount` is bare `numeric` (baseline `:600`), so `amount` matches it
rather than imposing a precision the parent column does not have.

Only **over-allocation** is rejected, by trigger, and the check must be
**sign-aware**: refunds carry a negative `total_amount`
(`spendingReport.ts:142` — "refunds stay negative"), so `sum <= total` is the wrong
test for a credit. Splitting a Receipt whose `total_amount` is `NULL` is refused
outright, as `validateAndComputeRemaining` already does (`ReceiptService.ts:566`).

A half-allocated receipt is a **legal, quiet state**: allocate the groceries, get
interrupted, and the rest simply keeps its original category. Nothing nags.

### Merging is how you un-split

Two splits of one Receipt can never name the same Category. Assigning a split to a
Category the Receipt already carries **merges** them and their amounts add — which
is also the undo: put a carve-off back to the remainder's Category and it rejoins
it. No separate gesture, no separate concept.

It destroys a deliberate division, so **it asks first**. The merged row is the
remainder if either input was, so a fully re-merged Receipt returns to exactly its
original one-row shape (`amount IS NULL`, whole total).

## Service layer

`ExpenseService.getExpenses` (`:119`) currently maps one row to one Expense
(`:126`) and `mapReceiptRowToExpense` (`:217`) reads `receipt.expense_categories`
as a **single object**. It fans out to one Expense per split, resolving the
remainder as it goes.

`Expense` (`:22`) gains an `id` and an `amount`; `receipt_id` stops identifying it.
`normalizedAmount` (`spendingReport.ts:143`) switches from `e.total_amount * rate`
to `e.amount * rate` — splits carry the **original** currency and the receipt's
stored rate, so foreign-currency handling falls out unchanged.

**The failure mode if this is done carelessly is silent.** `coerceEmbed` (`:95`) is
a bare `as T` cast with no runtime check. Give a receipt two category rows before
`getExpenses` understands them and PostgREST returns an _array_ — the category
resolves to `undefined`, the expense turns Uncategorized, and a $240 purchase
**vanishes from the Spending Report instead of throwing**. This is why the
conversion is verified against before/after report totals, not by tests alone.

Nothing else in the reporting layer changes. `buildSpendingReport` consumes
`SpendingExpense[]` where each row already has exactly one category and one amount
(`spendingReport.ts:32`), so a Category Split is **invisible** to it — it just sees
more rows. That property is why the model is 1:N rather than nested; see
[ADR-0008](../adr/0008-an-expense-is-a-portion-of-a-receipt.md).

## Two data-destruction paths close first

Neither is a new bug. Both are existing behaviour that only becomes destructive
once a Receipt can have several splits, and both must be closed **before** anything
can create a split.

### 1. Implicit vendor rules

`assignCategoryFromRow` auto-creates a vendor rule when a merchant has none
(`categoryAssignment.ts:95`), and the `apply_vendor_rule_after_insert` trigger then
applies it to every future receipt from that merchant.

So: click **Household** on the $60 Costco carve-off, and every Costco receipt your
family uploads from then on is auto-categorized Household. One click, silent,
family-wide, from a row visually identical to its neighbours.

**The side effect is switched off entirely for any Receipt with more than one
split.** Setting a merchant's default stays available as the deliberate,
explicitly-labelled act it should be (`CategoryDropdown.svelte:354`, UI at `:468`).
The shortcut costs almost nothing: once a family is set up, vendor rules rarely
change. It must not fire retroactively when a Receipt merges back down to one
split either.

The whole port is keyed on `receiptId` (`categoryAssignment.ts:19-37`), which is
simply ambiguous under 1:N, and `bulkAssignCategory` (`:72`) would violate
`unique(receipt_id, category_id)` the moment a selection held two splits of the
same Receipt — which the merge rule above resolves.

### 2. Bulk delete on the Expenses page

The code states the assumption it is about to lose:

```js
// #{#exp6b} Selection-based bulk delete. An expense IS a receipt (1:1, computed),
// so this deletes the underlying receipts (record + stored file).
```
`expenses/+page.svelte:171`

Under 1:N: tick the **$60 Household** row, press **"Delete Selected (1)"**, lose
the entire **$240 receipt and its image file**. The count says 1; three rows and
the image disappear. There is no undo anywhere in this app.

Root cause is that one selection served two operations wanting different
granularities — categorize wants splits, delete wants receipts. **Bulk delete moves
off the Expenses page.** An Expense is a view of part of a Receipt, so the only
coherent deletion is of the whole Receipt, which is a capture-surface act; the
Receipts page already has `deleteSelected` (`receipts/+page.svelte:541`).

## UI

### Expenses page — where splitting lives

Splitting happens **here and nowhere else**. It changes no field of the Receipt, so
the capture surface has no business offering it — one of the few places where
"Expenses for reporting, Receipts for capturing" holds cleanly rather than being
crossed for workflow reasons.

**One row per split.** The deciding argument is the category filter: with one row
per receipt, filtering to Household would show a **$240 row for a $60 purchase**,
and the page's totals would stop matching the Spending Report this feature exists
to feed. CSV and PDF export serialize `Expense[]` directly and inherit the fix.

Consequences for the table (`:1174-1189`):

- `getRowId={(e) => e.receipt_id}` (`:1192`) becomes the split's `id`. With a keyed
  list, leaving it is a hard failure, not a cosmetic one.
- Selection (`:188`) and `categoryByReceipt[expense.receipt_id]` (`:1156`) become
  per-split.
- Row click still opens the whole receipt (`:539`) — three rows, same modal, which
  is correct.
- **A visual grouping cue** so three Costco rows do not read as three purchases.
  It must look **different from reconciliation's "N of M" badge**
  (`reconciliation/+page.svelte:1064`), which means Partial Charge — reusing that
  idiom would rebuild in the UI exactly the confusion the rename removed from the
  language. A shared left-border / indent treatment, not a badge.
- **A new Actions column** with a "Split" link. The page has none today
  (Receipt / Date / Merchant / Amount / Category), while the Receipts page and
  reconciliation both do. All three Costco rows show the link and all three open
  the same modal: the action belongs to the Receipt, and any of its rows is a
  legitimate handle on it.

### The Category Split modal

**Separate from the receipt edit modal, deliberately.** There `total_amount` is a
live `bind:value` (`ReceiptEditModal.svelte:433`), so a split editor would validate
"these parts do not exceed the total" against a number being typed — delete the
total to retype it and every split is instantly over-allocated. The split modal
takes the total as **fixed** and asks one question: how is it divided?

Two supporting reasons: the edit modal is where the documented dropdown-clipping
trap lives (`overflow-y-auto` clipping absolutely-positioned menus in _both_ axes,
the bug that forced `@floating-ui/dom` in), and a split editor is _N_ dropdowns
rather than one; and it gives Category Split and Partial Charge parallel shapes,
which matters for two operations this easy to confuse.

The cost is honest: splitting a receipt _and_ fixing its amount means two modals.
Those are two different intentions.

### Receipts page — read-only

The Category column (`receipts/+page.svelte:1063`) renders `CategoryDropdown` with
`currentCategory={categoryMap[r.id] ?? null}` — a map keyed by receipt id holding
one category, which has no answer for a receipt with three.

For a split Receipt the cell goes **read-only**: "3 categories" (or chips), dropdown
disabled, pointing at the Expenses page. The alternatives were both traps —
changing only the remainder is a control that reports success while leaving
two-thirds of the receipt untouched, and collapsing the splits silently destroys
deliberate work from a control that gives no hint it is destructive.

The bonus: splits stay **discoverable** from the capture surface while reviewing an
upload batch, without being editable there.

Knock-on, deliberate: `applyAllVendorRules` only touches uncategorized rows, so a
split Receipt is **permanently out of reach of the retroactive vendor-rule sweep**.

## Partial Charge on a split Receipt

Rare — both operations on one Receipt is a rare² combination — and sized
accordingly: a guard and a sentence, not machinery.

Carving a Partial Charge off a split Receipt is **the same event as correcting its
total**, and behaves identically: the reduction lands on the remainder. Carve $40
off a $240 Costco trip with $60 + $30 carved off already, and the Groceries
remainder recomputes from $150 to $110 — it self-heals, which is the same property
that made the computed remainder attractive. Carve $200 and the remainder computes
to **−$50**, so the sign-aware over-allocation guard has to live on the Partial
Charge path too, not only the split path.

The reduction is silent unless the modal says so, so it must: **"Groceries:
$150 → $110."**

**The new Partial Charge Receipt inherits the parent's remainder Category** (and its
`categorization_source`). The money came out of the remainder, so it should carry
the remainder's category — otherwise the two halves of one shopping trip land in
different report buckets. This resolves the item punted in
[Classify on the Receipts Page](../plans-done/2026-08-03-classify-on-receipts-page-design.md#out-of-scope):
the previous default was the merchant's vendor rule, which overrides the most
recent human signal about that purchase.

Implementation wrinkle: the trigger is `AFTER INSERT` on `receipts`, so it fires
before client code can act. The client writes the `expense_categories` row
afterwards, overwriting the trigger's `auto` row — two writes, second wins, in the
safe direction per the "manual is never overwritten by auto" precedence. **The
trigger is left alone**; teaching it to skip receipts with a charge group would be
cleaner but leaves the part uncategorized if the client write then fails.

## Sequencing

**One change, not staged.** There are no users beyond the author's family, so the
staging that would let a regression be attributed to one layer is not worth four
deploys and two migrations.

Order within it still matters: rename first (nothing new written in the old
vocabulary), then the two destruction paths (before anything can create a split to
destroy), then the schema and `ExpenseService`, then the UI.

**Verify with `npm run db:reset` and compare the Spending Report's totals before
and after the 1:N conversion.** Every pre-existing row should produce identical
numbers — that is the whole value of the no-backfill property, and the silent
`coerceEmbed` failure mode is why it is checked by hand rather than trusted to
tests.

Version number is assigned by hand at commit time.

## Out of scope

- **Per-product itemization.** Splits are per-Category. Recording that the jeans
  cost $30 and the detergent $12 is a different feature with a different table.
- **A split's own note, date or image.** A Category Split has a category and an
  amount. Everything else belongs to the Receipt.
- **Reconciliation.** It matches Transaction ↔ Receipt on the receipt's total,
  which stays whole. No changes.
- **The window-scoped Partial Charge badge** (`product-backlog.md`) — unrelated,
  still open.

## Still open

- **The `#{#spl*}` spec-tag renaming scheme.** 11 tags, currently ambiguous between
  the two concepts.
- **The exact visual grouping cue** for split rows — the constraint (not a badge)
  is decided, the treatment is not.
- **Test strategy**, particularly for the remainder resolution and the sign-aware
  over-allocation guard on negative receipts.

The single working list — features, UX bugs, engineering, open questions, and
refactoring. Everything here is **open**: something a person could pick up.

**Completed work is deleted from this file, not annotated.** History lives in git,
in [ADRs](adr/) for decisions and rejected paths, in [`prd-done/`](prd-done/) for
finished PRDs, and in `CLAUDE.md` for anything that stays true and will bite

and remove the bullet. Refactoring items are summarized here as one-liners; the
full detail lives in [Refactoring backlog](refactoring-backlog.md), which is a
reference, not a separate to-do list.

## Features

- **Spending Report — remaining slices.** The report ships: table + chart views, cell drill-down, editable hierarchy (assign, re-parent, add & rename Groupings), assign-on-create, historical-expense import, **and year-over-year comparison** (table Change column + side-by-side prior-year bars) are all live. Also small and now live: the **"Year to Date" column heading is hardcoded**, so it reads wrong over an imported past year. **Not coming** — Importance-area CRUD (fixed at 3 areas, settled), Grouping delete/reorder, and the Bridge/waterfall ([ADR-0004](adr/0004-abandon-spending-bridge-waterfall-view.md)). See [Spending Report design](plans/2026-07-09-spending-report-design.md).
- **Receipt notes in the exports.** Deferred from [Receipt Notes](plans-done/2026-08-03-receipt-notes-design.md), which shipped without them. **CSV** is ~2 lines — one header entry plus one `escapeCSVField` call in `CSVExportService.buildRow` (`:79`); escaping already handles commas, quotes and newlines, and `parseExpenseImportCsv` ignores columns it does not need, so re-import is unaffected. - **Receipt image — rotate.** Rotate left and right anywhere a receipt is viewed.
- **Profile — manage emails.** Let users add/edit the email addresses associated with their account. This interacts with the unverified-alias security item below — verification is the fix, so design them together.

The read-only half already shipped — the Profile page lists family members via the `get_family_members()` RPC — so what remains is invite / accept / remove.

Open modelling question if this is built: dismissal is **pair-scoped** (you asserted A and B are distinct, so a later third copy still flags) vs **receipt-scoped** (mutes the receipt, and so hides the real duplicate when a third copy arrives) — pair-scoped looks right. **(2) Three scopes for one concept.** The row badge and yellow highlight are computed over the date-filtered list (`:396`), while the checkbox filter (`:317`) and the count badge (`:400`) are computed over `allReceipts`. So with a date filter on and the checkbox ticked, a receipt whose only partner sits outside the window is listed with no badge and no highlight; with the checkbox off, that same cross-boundary duplicate is silently invisible. **(3) Match rule is keyed on OCR's weakest field.** Exact `transaction_date` equality, when `resolveOcrReceiptDate` (`src/lib/utils/receiptDateCorrection.ts:186`) can rewrite an implausible date within a 90-day window — two photos of the same receipt can land on different dates and never group. It also ignores `merchant_name` (so $84.32 at Costco and $84.32 at the dentist on one day flag) and ignores `currency` (USD vs CAD same-day flags). Note a date _window_ breaks transitivity — A~B and B~C no longer implies A~C — so a "duplicate group" becomes a graph of pairs, an independent argument for pair-scoped dismissal. A file content hash would catch identical re-uploads with perfect precision but does nothing for two separate photos; additive, not a substitute. Punted 2026-07-26.

1	# Category Split — Design
2	
3	**Date:** 2026-08-04
4	**Status:** 📐 Designed, not built. Decided in a grilling session; the vocabulary and
5	invariants are already in [Domain model](../domain-model.md), and the structural
6	decision is [ADR-0008](../adr/0008-an-expense-is-a-portion-of-a-receipt.md).
7	
8	You shop at Costco and come home with $240 of groceries, cleaning supplies and a
9	pair of jeans. That is **one charge, one bank Transaction, one Receipt** — and
10	three kinds of spending. The app cannot say so. Its Category column holds exactly
11	one category, and the only division it offers carves the purchase into several
12	Receipts and destroys the reconciliation match to do it.
13	
14	## The word "split" was already taken, and it meant the opposite
15	
16	`splitReceipt` exists for **deferred charges** — a hotel deposit billed separately
17	from its balance, an AirBnB instalment, an order that ships in two parts. There
18	really are several bank Transactions, so carving the purchase into several full
19	Receipts is correct, and clearing `matched_transaction_id` on both
20	(`ReceiptService.ts:602`, `:637`) is the _point_: each part must now match its own
21	Transaction.
22	
23	Using that for a Costco trip would be wrong three times over. It fabricates
24	receipts that never existed. It destroys a match to express a reporting
25	preference. And because `detectDuplicates` keys on `amount|date` alone
26	(`duplicateDetection.ts:25`), an evenly-divided receipt immediately flags both
27	halves as Potential Duplicates on the very page you divided it.
28	
29	So the first change is vocabulary:
30	
31	|                                          | divides a purchase across | touches the match?      | frequency         |
32	| ---------------------------------------- | ------------------------- | ----------------------- | ----------------- |
33	| **Partial Charge** (was _Split Receipt_) | **Transactions**          | clears it, deliberately | rare              |
34	| **Category Split** (new)                 | **Categories**            | never                   | every Costco trip |
35	
36	Both names say what is being divided, and "split" survives only in the qualified
37	form. See the glossary entries in [Domain model](../domain-model.md).
38	
39	## Stage 0 — the rename
40	
41	Pure rename, no behaviour change, done first so nothing new is written in the old
42	vocabulary.
43	
44	- 411 occurrences of "split" outside the `.split()` string method, concentrated in
45	  three files: `ReceiptService.split.spec.ts` (145), `reconciliation/+page.svelte`
46	  (98), `ReceiptService.ts` (58).
47	- `receipts.split_group_id` → `charge_group_id` (baseline `:610`) and
48	  `idx_receipts_split_group_id` → `idx_receipts_charge_group_id` (`:781`). Both are
49	  metadata-only DDL — no data rewrite. There are **no generated Supabase types**;
50	  the models are hand-written (`src/lib/models/Receipt.ts`), so the DB surface is
51	  exactly those two objects plus 52 code references.
52	- The 11 `#{#spl*}` spec tags. Renaming scheme still open — see below.
53	- The hand-maintained baseline needs the two lines edited to match. Verify with
54	  `npm run db:reset`.
55	
56	**This is a breaking change with no compatibility window.** Vercel deploys on push;
57	`supabase db push` is a separate manual step, so code and schema disagree in
58	between. The blast radius is narrow and was checked: every read is `select('*')`,
59	so reads degrade silently to a `null` field, and only _writes_ of the column fail —
60	Partial Charge creation and its "N of M" badge. Nothing else in the app touches it.
61	Accepted rather than staged as expand-and-contract; push the migration as soon as
62	the deploy is green.
63	
64	## The model
65	
66	**An Expense becomes a categorized _portion_ of a Receipt.** A Receipt yields one
67	Expense per Category Split, and exactly one — carrying the whole total — when
68	nobody has split it, so the common case still reads 1:1.
69	
70	The Receipt is untouched. `total_amount` and `matched_transaction_id` are off
71	limits to this feature, which is why **reconciliation needs no changes at all**.
72	
73	### One split is the remainder
74	
75	You split by **carving off the exceptions**, not by describing every part. A Costco
76	trip already auto-categorized Groceries takes two actions to become
77	$150 Groceries / $60 Household / $30 Clothing, not three: you carve off Household
78	and Clothing, and Groceries keeps what is left.
79	
80	The remainder is **the row the Receipt already had**. Two things follow, and they
81	are the reason this design is cheap:
82	
83	- **No backfill.** Every row in `expense_categories` today is already a valid
84	  remainder with no siblings. The migration is additive and the existing data is
85	  correct by construction.
86	- **`categorization_source` survives.** A vendor rule's `auto` assignment is not
87	  silently converted to a manual one by carving $60 off it.
88	
89	### The remainder is computed, never stored
90	
91	`amount IS NULL` means "whatever is left" — `total_amount` minus its siblings,
92	resolved at read time.
93	
94	The deciding case is editing the receipt total. OCR reads $240; you carve off $60
95	Household; someone later corrects the total to $260 — and totals are editable from
96	**three** surfaces (the edit modal, the Expenses page, the Receipts page). With a
97	stored remainder the parts still sum to $240 against a $260 receipt and **nothing
98	errors**; the report quietly loses $20. Defined as what is left, the remainder
99	becomes $200 by construction. The same argument kills rounding drift: $10 in three
100	parts always adds up.
101	
102	The cost: `NULL` is a magic value needing a partial unique index, and **resolving
103	the remainder is a computation that must live in exactly one place**
104	(`ExpenseService`) or it will be reimplemented in the report, the exporters and the
105	split modal. `applyRuleToVisibleExpenses` exists today precisely because two pages
106	needed the same logic.
107	
108	### Schema
109	
110	```sql
111	ALTER TABLE expense_categories ADD COLUMN amount numeric;      -- NULL = the remainder
112	ALTER TABLE expense_categories DROP CONSTRAINT expense_categories_pkey;
113	ALTER TABLE expense_categories ADD COLUMN id uuid PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid();
114	ALTER TABLE expense_categories ADD CONSTRAINT expense_categories_receipt_category_unique
115	  UNIQUE (receipt_id, category_id);
116	CREATE UNIQUE INDEX expense_categories_one_remainder
117	  ON expense_categories (receipt_id) WHERE amount IS NULL;
118	```
119	
120	`receipts.total_amount` is bare `numeric` (baseline `:600`), so `amount` matches it
121	rather than imposing a precision the parent column does not have.
122	
123	Only **over-allocation** is rejected, by trigger, and the check must be
124	**sign-aware**: refunds carry a negative `total_amount`
125	(`spendingReport.ts:142` — "refunds stay negative"), so `sum <= total` is the wrong
126	test for a credit. Splitting a Receipt whose `total_amount` is `NULL` is refused
127	outright, as `validateAndComputeRemaining` already does (`ReceiptService.ts:566`).
128	
129	A half-allocated receipt is a **legal, quiet state**: allocate the groceries, get
130	interrupted, and the rest simply keeps its original category. Nothing nags.
131	
132	### Merging is how you un-split
133	
134	Two splits of one Receipt can never name the same Category. Assigning a split to a
135	Category the Receipt already carries **merges** them and their amounts add — which
136	is also the undo: put a carve-off back to the remainder's Category and it rejoins
137	it. No separate gesture, no separate concept.
138	
139	It destroys a deliberate division, so **it asks first**. The merged row is the
140	remainder if either input was, so a fully re-merged Receipt returns to exactly its
141	original one-row shape (`amount IS NULL`, whole total).
142	
143	## Service layer
144	
145	`ExpenseService.getExpenses` (`:119`) currently maps one row to one Expense

2	
3	Family expense tracking app built with SvelteKit 2, Svelte 5, Supabase, and Tailwind CSS 4.
4	
5	## Commands
6	
7	```bash
8	npm run dev          # Dev server on localhost:5173
9	npm run build        # Production build
10	npm run verify       # The whole gate: check → check:deno → lint → server tests
11	npm run check        # Type checking (svelte-check, warnings are errors)
12	npm run check:deno   # Type-check supabase/functions/ (Deno — outside tsconfig scope)
13	npm run test:unit    # Vitest, single run (browser + node projects)
14	npm run test:watch   # Vitest in watch mode
15	npm run test:e2e     # Playwright e2e tests
16	npm test             # Full test suite (unit + e2e)
17	npm run lint         # Prettier check + ESLint (incl. Tailwind classes; warnings are errors)
18	npm run lint:fix     # ESLint autofix — most Tailwind class findings are fixable
19	npm run format       # Auto-format with Prettier
20	```
21	
22	## Architecture
23	
24	- **Routes:** `src/routes/` — SvelteKit file-based routing
25	- **Services:** `src/lib/services/` — Business logic (ExpenseService, ReceiptService, etc.). Some use DI (take Supabase client as param), others use singleton pattern with module-level import.
26	- **Models:** `src/lib/models/` — TypeScript data models
27	- **Components:** `src/lib/components/` — Reusable Svelte components
28	- **Utils:** `src/lib/utils/` — Helper functions with co-located `.spec.ts` tests
29	- **Server:** `src/lib/server/` — Server-only code (file validation, OCR processing)
30	- **CSV Parsers:** `src/lib/services/csvParsers/` — Bank-specific CSV parsers (Amex, PC Financial, RBC, TD, Simplii, EQ Bank, Wealth Simple) with `BaseCSVParser` and `CSVParserFactory` for auto-detection
31	- **Docs:** `docs/` — Project documentation. `docs/adr/` (architecture decision records), `docs/plans/` (design docs — **when the work is done, `git mv` the plan to `docs/plans-done/`**, same reason and same depth as `prd-done/`, so its `../` links keep working; fix inbound links), `docs/prd-*.md` (active PRDs — in-file `**Status:**` front-matter carries the detail; **when a PRD is finished, `git mv` it to `docs/prd-done/`** so done-vs-active is visible from `ls` without opening files, and fix its now-one-level-deeper relative links plus any inbound links), `docs/product-backlog.md` (the single working list — features, bugs, engineering, and open refactoring items as one-liners) plus `docs/refactoring-backlog.md` (detailed RF-NN reference, not a separate to-do list), `docs/domain-model.md` (ubiquitous-language glossary). 32	- **Migrations:** `supabase/migrations/` — SQL migrations (schema + RLS policies)
33	
34	## Supabase Migrations
35	
36	Migrations live in `supabase/migrations/` as numbered SQL files. The project is linked to the remote Supabase project (`YFL Expense Tracker`, region `ca-central-1`).
37	
38	```bash
39	supabase migration list           # Show local vs remote migration status
40	supabase db push                  # Push pending migrations to remote database
41	supabase db push --dry-run        # Preview what would be applied without running
42	supabase migration new <name>     # Create a new empty migration file
43	supabase db diff --schema public  # Generate migration from local schema changes
44	supabase db reset                 # Reset local DB and re-run all migrations (destructive)
45	```

47	**Naming convention:** `YYYYMMDDHHMMSS_description.sql` — **14 digits, not 8** (e.g. `20260803120000_receipt_notes.sql`). 48	
49	**`supabase migration repair` edits bookkeeping only — it never runs or reverses SQL.** So its own suggestions are not safe to follow blindly: when local has a migration remote lacks, the CLI proposes `--status applied <version>`, which would record your _unapplied_ migration as done, and it then never runs. Before marking anything `applied`, confirm the schema object actually exists on remote (`select tgname from pg_trigger where …`, or check the column). Marking a version `reverted` deletes its history row without removing what it created, so pair it with a re-push of an idempotent migration or an `applied` repair under the corrected name. Prod history has now been repaired twice — once during the baseline squash, once for the 8-digit rename.

51	**Squashed to a baseline (2026-07-26).** `supabase/migrations/` holds one file,
52	`20260726120000_baseline.sql`; the 31 predecessors are in `supabase/migrations-archive/`. They
53	could not rebuild the DB from scratch — replay died at `007` with `relation "public.families" does

59	migration with `npm run db:reset` before pushing. See `docs/local-dev.md`.
60	
61	**Important:** The migration role does NOT own `storage.objects`, so `COMMENT ON POLICY` and `ALTER TABLE` on storage tables will fail. Stick to `CREATE POLICY` / `DROP POLICY` / `UPDATE storage.buckets` for storage changes.
62	
63	## Key Patterns
64	
65	- **Expenses are computed, not stored.** No "expenses" table — expenses are joins of receipts + expense*categories + categories. 67	- **All data is family-scoped.** Users belong to families via `family_members`. RLS policies enforce family-level access on receipts, transactions, categories, and vendor rules.

Today each receipt maps to exactly one expense (1:1), and that is enforced by the schema: `expense_categories_pkey PRIMARY KEY (receipt_id)`. **This is deliberately going away** — [ADR-0008](docs/adr/0008-an-expense-is-a-portion-of-a-receipt.md) makes an Expense a categorized \_portion* of a Receipt so one Costco trip can be $150 Groceries + $60 Household + $30 Clothing, designed in [Category Split](docs/plans/2026-08-04-category-split-design.md) and not yet built. Don't add code that assumes `receipt_id` identifies an expense row, and note that relaxing the key without teaching `ExpenseService` about it fails **silently**: `coerceEmbed` (`ExpenseService.ts:95`) is a bare `as T` cast, so a second category row makes PostgREST return an array, the expense turns Uncategorized, and the purchase vanishes from the Spending Report rather than throwing.
- **"Split" means two opposite things, and the vocabulary is mid-rename.** A **Partial Charge** (the shipped `splitReceipt` / `split_group_id`, renamed from _Split Receipt_) divides one purchase across several bank Transactions — a hotel deposit and its balance — and clears `matched_transaction_id` on purpose. A **Category Split** (designed, not built) divides one purchase across several Categories and must **never** touch `total_amount` or the match. Reusing one for the other destroys reconciliation data. Definitions in [Domain model](docs/domain-model.md); the code still says `split` for the Partial Charge everywhere until the rename lands.

- **All data is family-scoped.** Users belong to families via `family_members`. RLS policies enforce family-level access on receipts, transactions, categories, and vendor rules.

All written and verified — no broken links, Prettier clean, no code touched.

## What I created

**[`docs/adr/0008-an-expense-is-a-portion-of-a-receipt.md`](docs/adr/0008-an-expense-is-a-portion-of-a-receipt.md)** — why the 1:1 dies. Context, the four rejected alternatives (nested allocations, a hybrid table, stored remainders, exact-balance enforcement), and the consequences, including the silent `coerceEmbed` failure mode and the two destruction paths.

**[`docs/plans/2026-08-04-category-split-design.md`](docs/plans/2026-08-04-category-split-design.md)** — the implementation shape: the rename with its no-compatibility-window analysis, the schema DDL, the remainder rules, the service-layer fan-out, both destruction paths with the code that proves them, the UI on all three surfaces, the Partial Charge interaction, sequencing, and what's still open.

## What I amended

- **`CLAUDE.md`** — the 1:1 Key Pattern now says it's true *today* and scheduled to go, with the silent-failure warning; plus a new pattern on the two meanings of "split".
- **`docs/domain-model.md`** — written continuously through the session: **Partial Charge** (renamed), **Category Split** (new), **Receipt** and **Expense** rewritten, and four new invariants (remainder, merge-is-undo, no-implicit-vendor-rule, Partial-Charge-on-split).
- **`docs/product-backlog.md`** — Category Split added as a Feature; the "what does a split inherit" item **deleted** (resolved, per the file's own delete-don't-annotate rule); the window-scoped badge item re-termed to Partial Charge.
- **`docs/refactoring-backlog.md`** — a terminology note at the top; landed entries left as-is, since that file is a historical record.
- **`docs/plans-done/2026-08-03-classify-on-receipts-page-design.md`** — its "Out of scope" punt marked resolved, noting this design also reverses its premise for splitting.

## Two things worth flagging

**Your original question answered itself in the negative.** You asked what a clickable split on the Receipts page implies; the answer is that it shouldn't go there — a Category Split changes no field of the Receipt, so it belongs on the reporting surface. Worth knowing that's where we landed, because it's the opposite of the starting assumption.

**The two destructive paths are pre-existing, not new.** Bulk delete on the Expenses page and implicit vendor-rule creation are shipped and working correctly *today* — they only become data-destroying once a receipt can have several splits. The design orders them before the schema change for that reason, but they're also worth knowing about independently of whether this feature ever gets built.
